text: An orbit that goes around the Earth 8.05 times a day with an eccentricity of 0.25 (the exact 8:1 resonance with the Earth's rotation) is predicted 1.3 km off along its track 7 days after a fit, against 94 to 220 m just either side of it: no part of the model carries that resonance's gravity terms.

On seven real windows of the TESS space telescope (an orbit of 13.7 days that reaches the Moon's distance), predictions from 72-hour fits to its reference's 10-minute solution states are a median 0.39 km off after one day, 1.9 km after three days and 15.4 km after a week, and 0.81 km ahead of SGP4-XP at three days. The test also holds them to the archived 0.77 km at one day and 7.6 km at a week. That comparison is scored the way the archive was, on a reading in which half the states are the reference files' straight-line fill between those solution states, up to about 1 km off the orbit, and there they are 1.01 and 9.0 km. TESS fires its thrusters about weekly, by 7 to 11 mm/s. In six of the seven windows a firing lies in the 72-hour fit arc (four windows) or within 13 hours after it (two); 10 mm/s moves the orbit by about 4 km in five days, so past a firing the error measures the firing as much as the prediction. In six of the seven windows the reference changes from one ephemeris file to the next 13 hours after the cutoff, with a step of 17 to 221 m.

On a 7-day arc of an eccentric orbit with drag (Molniya), the record states the drag coefficient to 0.09 % while the fitted value is 0.3 to 0.5 % from the truth: the stated uncertainty is 5 to 7 times too small; its position covariance is honest.

At some perigee passages of eccentric orbits, the SGP4-XP theory gives a wrong position for a few milliseconds, where the US Space Force library's positions are smooth. Of ten eccentric orbits flown every millisecond through two perigee passages each, two show it at both passages: an orbit of eccentricity 0.5 going around the Earth 4 times a day (7 ms per passage, up to 0.79 km off) and one of eccentricity 0.9 going around every two days (5 to 6 ms, up to 134,000 km off). Positions taken at random times, as the rest of the conformance test takes them, almost never fall in such a window.
